hints: Measure the time for one complete cycle by comparing two consecutive points in the same phase, such as neighbouring crests.
Convert the period from milliseconds to seconds before taking its reciprocal.
walkthrough: A complete cycle runs from the crest at t = 0 ms to the next crest at t = 4.0 ms.
The period is therefore T = 4.0 ms = 4.0 × 10⁻³ s.
This gives f = 250 Hz.

ai_rubric.observable: Reads a period of 4.0 ms, or 4.0 × 10⁻³ s, from the graph.
Uses the reciprocal of the period to obtain a frequency of 250 Hz.

hints: Read the reference-wave amplitude and period from Fig. 5.1 before changing either feature.
Use the squared amplitude relationship to find the new amplitude from the intensity ratio 2I/I.
A 90° phase difference is one quarter of a cycle, so convert one quarter of the period into a time shift.
walkthrough: From Fig. 5.1, wave X has amplitude 2.0 cm and period 4.0 ms.
For intensity proportional to amplitude squared, I_Z/I_X = (A_Z/A_X)².
Wave Z has the same frequency as X, so retain the 4.0 ms period.
A phase difference of 90° is one quarter of a cycle: 4.0 ms / 4 = 1.0 ms.
Draw a sinusoidal curve of amplitude 2.8 cm and period 4.0 ms, shifted 1.0 ms either left or right relative to wave X.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses intensity proportional to amplitude squared to determine an amplitude of about 2.8 cm.
Draws a sinusoidal trace with the same period as wave X and amplitude about 2.8 cm.
Shifts the trace by 1.0 ms to either side of wave X, corresponding to 90°.

hints: Choose two well-separated points on the line and convert the fringe-width change from millimetres to metres before calculating the gradient.
From x = λD/a, the gradient of x against D is λ/a; multiply the gradient by the known slit separation.
walkthrough: Read two points from the line: D = 1.75 m gives x = 2.4 mm, and D = 3.25 m gives x = 4.5 mm.
Convert the fringe-width change to metres: Δx = (4.5 − 2.4) × 10⁻³ = 2.1 × 10⁻³ m.
Calculate the gradient: Δx/ΔD = (2.1 × 10⁻³)/(3.25 − 1.75) = 1.4 × 10⁻³.
For double-slit interference, x = λD/a, so the graph gradient is λ/a.
The slit separation is a = 0.45 mm = 0.45 × 10⁻³ m, so λ = a × gradient.
Convert to nanometres: 6.3 × 10⁻⁷ m = 630 nm.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates a graph gradient of about 1.4 × 10⁻³ using correctly converted fringe-width values.
Uses the double-slit relationship to multiply the gradient by the 0.45 mm slit separation.

hints: Express the double-slit relationship as x = (λ/a)D so the graph gradient can be identified.
Keep the wavelength fixed and consider how increasing the denominator a changes both the gradient and the fringe width at a given D.
walkthrough: The double-slit relationship can be written x = (λ/a)D.
On an x–D graph, the gradient is therefore λ/a.
Increasing the slit separation a decreases λ/a because the wavelength is unchanged.
The new line has a smaller positive gradient than the original line.
For every distance D, the fringe width x is smaller, so the new line lies completely below the original line.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that increasing slit separation reduces λ/a and hence reduces the graph gradient.
States that fringe width is reduced at every D, so the new line lies below the original line or has a lower intercept.
